title: Residence time of a pollutant in a well-mixed lake
summary: A constant pollutant load approaches a steady mass equal to load times the lake's residence time.
question: How long does a lake take to reach steady pollution, and how much pollutant does it hold then?
teaching: A single mass stock gains pollutant at 50 kg/day and loses it through the outflow at the well-mixed concentration. With V = 1e7 m3 and Q = 1e5 m3/day, the residence time V/Q is 100 days, so the steady mass is 5,000 kg and the concentration is 0.5 mg/L. The mass reaches 63 % of steady state after one residence time, the signature of a first-order box model.

references.citation: Harte, J. (1988). Consider a Spherical Cow: A Course in Environmental Problem Solving. University Science Books.

title: Exponential growth and the rule of 70
summary: Exponential growth at 2 % per year doubles a population in about 35 years, as the rule of 70 estimates.
question: How many times does a population double in a century at a 2 % annual growth rate?
teaching: A single population stock grows at r*P with r = 0.02 per year. The exact doubling time is ln(2)/r = 34.66 years, while the rule of 70 gives 35 years; both are shown as converters, along with the number of doublings completed. After 100 years the population is e^2 = 7.39 million and has completed 2.89 doublings.

references.citation: Harte, J. (1988). Consider a Spherical Cow: A Course in Environmental Problem Solving. University Science Books.

title: Lake phosphorus: Vollenweider steady state
summary: A phosphorus mass balance with flushing and sedimentation settles at the loading rate divided by total loss.
question: What phosphorus concentration should a lake reach for a given external load, flushing rate and sedimentation rate?
teaching: The water-column phosphorus mass gains the external load and loses (rho + sigma)*M, where rho is the flushing rate Q/V and sigma is sedimentation. With a 1,000 kg/yr load, a 0.5 per year flushing rate and a 0.5 per year sedimentation rate, the loss rate is 1 per year and the steady concentration is 100 ug/L. The approach time is 1 year, so the lake reaches 63 % of steady state after one year.

references.citation: Harte, J. (1988). Consider a Spherical Cow: A Course in Environmental Problem Solving. University Science Books.
Vollenweider, R. A. (1975). Input-output models with special reference to the phosphorus loading concept in limnology. Schweizerische Zeitschrift für Hydrologie, 37(1), 53–84.

title: Bioconcentration of a contaminant in fish
summary: A fish takes up a water contaminant until depuration balances uptake, then clears it with a 6.9-day half-life when exposure stops.
question: How high does a contaminant build up in fish tissue, and how fast does it leave after exposure ends?
teaching: One fish-concentration stock gains k1*C_water and loses k2*C_fish, giving a bioconcentration factor k1/k2 = 5,000 L/kg and a steady tissue concentration of 5,000 ug/kg. The time to 95 % of steady state is 3/k2 = 30 days. Exposure stops at day 60; the depuration half-life is ln(2)/k2 = 6.93 days, so tissue concentration halves in about a week.

references.citation: Harte, J. (1988). Consider a Spherical Cow: A Course in Environmental Problem Solving. University Science Books.
Mackay, D. (1982). Correlation of bioconcentration factors. Environmental Science & Technology, 16(5), 274–278.

title: Radon in a house
summary: Soil-gas radon entering a house balances ventilation and radioactive decay at a steady indoor concentration.
question: How much does reducing the air-exchange rate raise indoor radon?
teaching: A radon-activity stock gains a constant soil-gas entry and loses activity through ventilation and radioactive decay. In a 300 m3 house with 0.5 air changes per hour, the steady concentration is 19.7 Bq/m3; a tight house with 0.1 air changes per hour approaches 92.9 Bq/m3. The approach time is 1.97 h, so the normal house is essentially at steady state within 48 hours.

references.citation: Harte, J. (1988). Consider a Spherical Cow: A Course in Environmental Problem Solving. University Science Books.
Nazaroff, W. W. (1992). Radon transport from soil to air. Reviews of Geophysics, 30(2), 137–160.
